title: Networking
whyItMatters: Every request a frontend makes crosses this layer. Most 'slow page' answers live here.

questions.prompt: What does `Cache-Control: no-cache` tell the browser to do?
options: Never store the response at all
Store it, but revalidate with the server before reusing it
Store it for the default heuristic lifetime
Store it only in memory, never on disk
questions.explanation: no-cache stores the response but forces revalidation; no-store is the directive that refuses to write it down at all.

concept.title: no-cache is not no-store
concept.summary: The two directives sound alike and do almost opposite things.
points: no-store: never written to any cache. Used for sensitive responses.
no-cache: cached, but every reuse needs a revalidation round trip.
A revalidation that returns 304 still costs latency, just not bandwidth.
max-age=0, must-revalidate behaves close to no-cache.

questions.prompt: What limitation did HTTP/2 multiplexing address compared with ordinary HTTP/1.1 browser connections?
options: Responses could not be compressed
Each connection normally handled one active request at a time, so browsers opened several connections and queued excess work
Requests could not be encrypted
Cookies had to be sent on every request
questions.explanation: Without pipelining, an HTTP/1.1 connection normally carries one active request at a time. Browsers therefore open a small pool of connections per origin and queue excess work, while HTTP/2 multiplexes independent streams over one connection.

concept.title: Head-of-line blocking, twice
concept.summary: Each HTTP version moved the queue somewhere else rather than removing it.
points: Ordinary HTTP/1.1 browser use: one active request per connection, a small connection pool per origin, then queuing.
HTTP/2: many streams on one TCP connection, so no application-level queue.
But a lost TCP packet still stalls every stream, because TCP delivers in order.
HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP so one lost packet only stalls its own stream.

questions.prompt: Which request triggers a CORS preflight?
options: A cross-origin GET with no custom headers
A cross-origin POST sending JSON with Content-Type: application/json
A same-origin PUT
Any request that sets a cookie
questions.explanation: application/json is not a CORS-safelisted content type, so the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight first.

concept.title: What makes a request 'simple'
concept.summary: A cross-origin request skips the preflight only if it stays inside a narrow safelist.
points: Method must be GET, HEAD or POST.
Content-Type must be form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain.
No custom request headers such as Authorization or X-Request-Id.
Anything outside that sends an OPTIONS preflight the server must answer.

questions.prompt: What does TCP give you that UDP does not?
options: Encryption of the payload
Ordered, retransmitted delivery
Lower latency on first connection
Compression of the payload
questions.explanation: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream with retransmission and congestion control. UDP provides independent datagrams without delivery or ordering guarantees; its smaller transport contract can reduce overhead, but application behavior and network conditions determine actual latency and loss handling.

concept.title: TCP vs UDP
concept.summary: TCP trades latency for guarantees. Neither one encrypts anything.
points: TCP: handshake, ordered delivery, retransmission, congestion control.
UDP: datagrams with no transport-level ordering, retransmission, or connection handshake.
Encryption is TLS, a separate layer, available over both.
Video calls and QUIC pick UDP and rebuild only the guarantees they need.

questions.prompt: What does validating a server certificate during a TLS handshake establish?
options: That the connection is encrypted
That the presented public key is authorized for the requested hostname under a trusted certificate chain
That the payload has not been compressed
That the client is who it says it is
questions.explanation: Certificate validation checks a trusted chain, validity constraints, and whether the certificate identifies the requested hostname; the handshake also proves possession of the corresponding private key. This authenticates the service identity, not legal ownership of the domain. Traffic keys are established by the handshake.

concept.title: What TLS does in what order
concept.summary: Identity first, then a shared secret, then encrypted traffic.
points: Server presents a certificate chaining to a CA the client trusts.
Client verifies the chain and that the domain matches.
Both derive a shared symmetric key without ever sending it.
Traffic from then on is symmetric-encrypted, which is the fast part.

questions.prompt: A browser holds a response with an ETag. What does it send on the next request?
options: The full response body for comparison
An If-None-Match header carrying that ETag
A Cache-Control: no-store header
Nothing — it serves from cache without contacting the server
questions.explanation: If-None-Match lets the server reply 304 with no body when the resource is unchanged.

concept.title: Revalidation saves bytes, not round trips
concept.summary: A 304 is still a full network round trip.
points: ETag is an opaque version tag the server chose.
If-None-Match asks: has it changed since this version?
304 Not Modified: no body, but you still paid the latency.
Only a fresh max-age avoids the network entirely.

questions.prompt: Why is shipping a 301 riskier than a 302?
options: 301 is slower to process
301 declares a permanent move and can be cached, so clients and intermediaries may keep using a mistaken target
301 drops query parameters
301 cannot be used with HTTPS
questions.explanation: A 301 declares a permanent move and is cacheable unless cache controls say otherwise, so a wrong target can persist in clients or intermediaries. A 302 describes a temporary redirect, although its caching still depends on HTTP cache rules and response headers.

concept.title: Redirects you can and cannot undo
concept.summary: The permanence is a promise to the client, not just a label.
points: 301 / 308: permanent redirects that can be cached and are harder to reverse once reused.
302 / 307: temporary redirects; cache behavior still follows response headers and HTTP caching rules.
307 and 308 preserve the method; 301 and 302 historically did not.
Use 302 while you are unsure, 301 once the move is final.

questions.prompt: Where does a browser look first when resolving a hostname?
options: The authoritative nameserver for the domain
Its own and the OS cache, before any network query
The root nameservers
The nearest CDN edge node
questions.explanation: Resolution walks outward from local caches; the recursive resolver only queries the hierarchy on a miss.

concept.title: DNS resolution, outward
concept.summary: Every layer is a cache, which is why DNS changes take time to appear.
points: Browser cache, then OS cache, then the configured resolver.
Resolver misses walk root → TLD → authoritative nameserver.
Each answer carries a TTL that decides how long it is reused.
That TTL is why a DNS cutover is planned hours ahead.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a different origin from `https://app.example.com/dashboard`?
options: https://app.example.com/settings
https://app.example.com:8443/dashboard
https://app.example.com/dashboard?tab=1
https://app.example.com/dashboard#top
questions.explanation: An origin is scheme, host and port. The path, query and fragment are not part of it, but a different port is a different origin.

concept.title: Origin = scheme + host + port
concept.summary: Three parts, and all three must match.
points: https vs http is a different origin, even on the same host.
A different port is a different origin, including 443 vs 8443.
Subdomains are different origins: app.example.com ≠ example.com.
Path, query and hash never affect the origin.

questions.prompt: HTTP/3 runs over UDP instead of TCP. What did that buy?
expects: names TCP head-of-line blocking as the problem
mentions the faster handshake or connection migration
questions.probeIfMissing: What happens to the other streams when one TCP packet is lost?

concept.title: Why QUIC left TCP behind
concept.summary: HTTP/2 removed the application queue but inherited TCP's.
points: TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls every HTTP/2 stream on that connection.
QUIC tracks streams itself, so loss only stalls the stream it belongs to.
QUIC folds the TLS handshake in, cutting a round trip on connect.
Connections are identified by an ID, so they survive a network change.

questions.prompt: A response is in the browser cache but the request still hits the network. Why?
expects: connects it to a directive such as no-cache or max-age=0
questions.probeIfMissing: What is the difference between a cached response and a fresh one?

concept.title: Cached is not the same as fresh
concept.summary: The cache decides reuse by freshness, not by presence.
points: Fresh (inside max-age): served with no network at all.
Stale or no-cache: revalidated with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since.
304 means the body is reused, but the round trip already happened.
stale-while-revalidate serves the old copy and refreshes in the background.

questions.prompt: The API is fast in Postman but slow in the browser. Where do you look?
expects: separates server time from everything around it
names at least two browser-only costs such as CORS preflight, TLS, DNS or connection limits
describes how they would confirm it rather than guessing
questions.probeIfMissing: What does the browser do before the request that Postman does not?

concept.title: What the browser adds
concept.summary: Same endpoint, very different work around it.
points: A preflight OPTIONS doubles the round trips on every call.
Cold DNS, TCP and TLS can cost more than the response itself.
Per-origin connection limits queue requests on HTTP/1.1.
The waterfall in devtools splits all of this out — read it before guessing.

questions.prompt: Your team added an Authorization header and latency doubled. Why would that happen?
expects: connects the custom header to a CORS preflight
explains the extra OPTIONS round trip
mentions caching the preflight with Access-Control-Max-Age
questions.probeIfMissing: What does the browser send before the real request now?

concept.title: A header that costs a round trip
concept.summary: A custom header pushes the request out of the CORS safelist.
points: Authorization is not safelisted, so every call now preflights.
That is an extra OPTIONS round trip before the real one.
Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the preflight result.
Same-origin requests never preflight, which is why a proxy path also fixes it.

questions.prompt: You shipped a fix. It works for you but users still report the old behaviour. Where do you look?
expects: names caching at some layer as the likely cause
distinguishes browser cache, CDN and service worker
proposes how to confirm which layer is serving the stale copy
questions.probeIfMissing: How many places between your server and that user could be holding the old file?

concept.title: Every layer holds a copy
concept.summary: 'Works for me' usually means your cache cleared and theirs did not.
points: Browser cache, service worker, CDN edge and origin each keep their own copy.
A service worker can serve stale assets long after a hard refresh.
Content-hashed filenames make each deploy a new URL, sidestepping all of it.
Check the response headers on the user's request, not yours.
